The ropemoss on the sill's north face, which had fruited every autumn within living memory, had not fruited for eleven years. Five explanations were current in the valley: that the tenant had begun wintering sheep on the top; that a stand of larch which had shaded the face had been felled; that run-off from a newly cut footpath had changed the way water crosses the sill; that lime dust from the widened quarry road was settling on the leaves; and that the spring feeding the face had been dammed to fill a cattle trough.

Nobody had written the fruiting down on purpose. The estate's game book keeps the dates of the shoot and nothing else. The hotel at Cleave Bridge threw out its guest album when it changed hands. The schoolmaster's weather diary, which runs from 1948, notes frost and rainfall and never the face. The water company's inspection sheets begin only in 2009. The dates survive in one place: the minutes of the Cleave Valley flower show, where for sixty years the secretary set down what the north face was doing on the morning of the judging.

The party laid out five plots along the face and read each one three times a summer, keeping a close watch on the youngest growth in particular, since the fruiting bodies appear there first. Plot four went unread in the second summer. The markers were all standing when the party came back in August; the track was dry the whole of that June; the top gate has never carried a lock; and nothing has burned on the sill since 1976. The party's June week that year fell inside the fortnight when the tenant shuts the top ground while the lambs are small.

A dust gauge stands at the quarry and is emptied and weighed every Friday, and the party asked for its readings — not to measure what was settling on the moss, which they took from the leaves themselves, but because the gauge carries a vane and a record of the week's wind, and the party wanted to know which of its five plots lay downwind of the road.

Four of the five explanations did not survive the plots. Fruiting failed on the two plots the sheep cannot reach as badly as on the three they can. It failed as badly where the larches had thrown their shade as in the plots still shaded by the rock. It failed in the two plots upwind of the road as badly as in the three downwind. Where the new path throws its water, fruiting failed no worse than where the path throws none. What separates the plots is September wetting, and the face has not been wet in September since the spring was taken for the trough; the two plots nearest the old seep line are the only ones that have fruited at all.

The party will not say more than that. Harrow Sill is one face on one hill, and the report's second sentence and its last both decline to speak for Lyn Scar, or for the sills above Deddon, or for any north face but this one.

Between 1904 and 1931 Bettina Kraal made glass eyes for the museum trade in a first-floor room above a chandler's in Halder, and the colours she mixed have never been matched since. Every account of her ends with the same complaint: that her ledger of recipes was lost. Five fates have been proposed for it in print. It burned with the stock in the warehouse fire of 1938. It went with the lease to the firm that took the premises, and stands unacknowledged behind that firm's catalogue. An apprentice copied it out, and the original went down with the copyist on the Trevone. The family kept it, and for fifty years nobody opened it. It was given to a county museum and entered in the register under the name of the donor rather than the maker.

She would not begin an order until she had been told which room the mount was to stand in and which way its windows faced, and she asked the same two questions of a duke's agent and of a grammar school. A hen harrier for a north-lit corridor and a hen harrier for a bay window were not, in her account books, the same commission, and were not the same price.

A pawn ticket for her bench lathe, made out in March 1931 and redeemed in the July, is the only reason we can say when the workshop stopped taking orders. She entered none after that spring, the numbered series ends at 2,411, and the two eyes sometimes dated to 1933 carry numbers from within the series and were therefore made earlier.

Her work was not identified in any public collection until 1974, and not by a curator. An insurance assessor valuing the Sallow Museum's bird gallery after a burst pipe turned a case around, read the initials scratched inside a socket, and wrote them into his schedule as a curiosity. The museum's own catalogue had carried the gallery as "continental, maker unknown" since 1911.

What has never been matched is the winter grey, which carries a faint green cast in daylight and none at all under a lamp. Aldous Penn in 1962 and Marie Ostrow in 1988 each spent years reconstructing it from the mounts themselves, grinding and firing and comparing, and each published a formula that is not hers.

The ledger was eleven minutes' walk from the room it was written in. It sat on a shelf in her niece's house, in the same town, through both reconstructions, and neither scholar wrote to the family, because both had read in print that it was lost.
